title: How NOT to build control-target gates in semiconductor quantum dots and beyond
authors: Roman Korol, John Nichol, Ignacio Franco
abstract: Universal quantum computation requires single-qubit control together with at least one entangling two-qubit gate. CNOT and CROT gates are two famous examples of such gates, wherein the state of one qubit (control) dictates the transformation applied to the other (target). By using a simple derivation motivated by symmetry, we show that current device architectures of semiconductor-based quantum dot devices prevent efficient implementation of a CNOT and other asymmetric control-target gates via Heisenberg exchange, Coulomb repulsion, or other interaction that is invariant under spin exchange. Guided by this general principle, we propose a heterogeneous blueprint of double quantum dot devices that enables efficient implementation of the CNOT by breaking the spin exchange symmetry. Crucially, our numerical simulations predict that this novel device blueprint can enable a single-pulse fault-tolerant 100-ns CNOT gate in isotopically purified silicon.
summary: This paper tackles the challenge of building asymmetric two-qubit gates, such as CNOT, in semiconductor quantum dots. The authors prove that natural interactions are too symmetric for these gates and propose a novel heterogeneous device blueprint. This design breaks the necessary symmetry, enabling high-fidelity, fast CNOT operations purely through electrical control.
main_problem: The primary challenge is implementing efficient, asymmetric two-qubit gates (like CNOT) in semiconductor quantum dot qubits.
main_result: The authors propose a heterogeneous double quantum dot blueprint that breaks spin exchange symmetry, enabling a single-pulse, fault-tolerant CNOT gate predicted for isotopically purified silicon within 100 ns.
method: They use theoretical analysis based on symmetry constraints to argue that homogeneous architectures fail for asymmetric gates, leading them to design a hardware solution using non-identical qubit encodings.
model_or_system: The system is semiconductor quantum dots, modeled using the Fermi-Hubbard model and mapped to a spin Hamiltonian. The focus is on singlet-triplet qubits within double quantum dot architectures.
key_observables: CNOT gate fidelity ($>99\%$), gate time ($\sim 100 	ext{ ns}$), and the preservation of coherence in isotopically purified silicon.
important_parameters: The key physical parameters involve the exchange coupling ($J_{ij}$) and the ability to break spin-exchange symmetry via heterogeneous device design.
main_assumptions: It is assumed that single-qubit gates are highly accurate, and the derivation relies on projecting interactions onto a computational subspace while accounting for leakage.
figures_summary: Not specified in detail; the notes focus on theoretical derivations regarding Hamiltonian symmetry and proposed device blueprints rather than figure descriptions.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the necessity of asymmetric gates, then theoretically proves that symmetric interactions prevent these gates in homogeneous systems. It proposes a heterogeneous blueprint to break this symmetry, culminating in numerical simulations predicting high-fidelity gate operation.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses hardware limitations in solid-state quantum computing by showing how architectural design (heterogeneity) can be used as a resource to overcome fundamental physical symmetries that restrict gate operations.
